prose.note: The manuscript offers tactile, controlled imagery—corroded batteries, wet tape, split soles, and voices reduced to physical media—and sustains strong sentence rhythm. It overuses aphoristic reversals and fragments such as “Not clean. Clean enough,” however, until the technique becomes conspicuous.

continuity.note: The central plot remains coherent, but scarce objects are tracked unreliably: Mara’s revolver inexplicably rises from two rounds to four, lost knives reappear, Nico’s antibiotics vanish, and the final account conflates distinct rings. These are especially damaging in a novel that makes exact inventory a moral and dramatic principle.

structure.note: The signal’s progression from possible rescue to edited bait to the living Elias is well staged, and the hospital climax grows from established choices rather than arbitrary escalation. The final act runs through several successive climaxes—relay fire, basement breach, rooftop sacrifice, Rowan’s defeat, Tamsin’s stand, and Elias’s mercy killing—which dilutes the force of individual beats.

voice.note: Mara’s inventory-minded narration remains remarkably consistent from battery shed to final watch, without significant late-book drift. Distinction among speakers is weaker: Mara, Tamsin, Nico, and at times Elias all favor the same clipped corrections, dry reversals, and “math/inventory/clean” vocabulary.

payoff.note: The manuscript strongly resolves its primary promises: the coordinate error, repeated breaths, hold phrase, yellow ambulance, tapes, last bullet, Nico’s complicity, Tamsin’s betrayal, and empty final frequency all pay off. The early medicine stakes are weakened when Maeve and Gide disappear from the operative ledger, replacement patient names proliferate, and the antibiotics traded to Nico are never accounted for.

judgement.verdict: This is a cohesive, often gripping survival novel with unusually strong thematic integration: radios, records, ammunition, and procedure all become instruments of both rescue and harm, and Elias’s adult reveal earns its bleak emotional force. What most limits it is not the main architecture but faulty object and character accounting—particularly ammunition, weapons, medicine, injuries, and Dunbar’s patients—in a story whose entire authority depends on exact counts.

issues.description: Mara begins with five revolver rounds, fires twice in Chapter 2 and once in Chapter 4, leaving two; yet intake opens her cylinder and removes “Four rounds.” The later climax then restores the two-round count without explaining any reload.

Mara leaves her knife embedded in a stalker’s skull during the drainage fight, but soon afterward “cut[s] the coil in half with her knife” at Nico’s toll. Chapter 5 again has her cut open the Portland crate with a knife, and Chapter 6 confiscates a folding knife, fixed blade, and boot blade despite those weapons never being acquired or restored.

The antibiotic packet Tamsin steals and trades to Nico in Chapter 3 disappears from the story. Nico later joins the party while Tamsin has a serious rebar wound, but no one considers the drugs, and Rowan’s detailed intake inventory of Nico’s possessions omits them entirely.

The final office scene calls the recovered object “Nico’s ring from the toll shrine” and says Mara took it after his pack spilled. At the shrine there are two rings on a key loop; later Nico separately produces a single ring from his pocket and says it came from the travelers’ pack, and neither Mara’s recovery nor a spilled pack is shown.

Dunbar’s medical stakes lose continuity. Chapter 1 specifically establishes Maeve’s nine-day insulin supply and Gide’s cough, but Tamsin later invokes Harlan’s chest, Bea’s boy, Jonah, Kep, Mina, Sella’s lungs, and Hark’s wound; Maeve’s urgent fuse is never revisited.

Tamsin’s established injury is a long forearm laceration from rebar, but subsequent narration repeatedly describes her pressing a bandaged or bleeding “side” before the later fight supplies any clear torso wound. The injury migrates anatomically according to scene needs.

The recurring boot inventory changes feet without explanation. Mara abandons her original right-split boot and adopts maintenance boots with a split left sole, which later causes repeated trouble; during the return, the manuscript again says her right boot has split from toe to ball.

Nico joins the protagonists only “two streets after the dry cleaner,” ostensibly because their gunshot threatens his route, then accompanies them all the way to First Hill without the promised renegotiation or a clearly stated goal. His eventual sacrifice works thematically, but the alliance that gets him there is under-motivated.

The climax accumulates too many discrete terminal crises: archive burning, lower-ward breach, rooftop antenna sabotage and Nico’s death, Rowan’s attempted escape, Tamsin’s confession and stand, then Elias’s mercy killing. Each is prepared, but their uninterrupted sequence makes the chapter feel serially escalated rather than sharply focused.

Mara, Tamsin, Nico, and Elias frequently share the same rhetorical machinery: clipped fragments, dry correction of the previous sentence, and repeated appeals to “math,” “inventory,” “clean,” and “useful.” This blurs otherwise distinct character backgrounds.
